kolu under any chat app

Comparisons·seedling·proposed·JUL 13, 2026

The coding agent has moved into the chat. kolu is the open, model-agnostic terminal/file foundation any chat app integrates — and the model is a mirror of the coordinator: observe flows out raw (the who-needs-me board), act flows in through one disciplined orchestrator agent, and the same door makes the coordinator a grounded participant in the humans' own discussion. The first proof is an XS bot binding a thread to the coordinator that already runs kolu's own development.

A read of Anthropic’s Claude Tag (Claude joins the team chat as a tagged teammate) and AI researcher Andrej Karpathy’s framing of it as “the 3rd major redesign of LLM UIUX,” held against what kolu is. Throughout, XS stands for any chat app (a Slack-style team chat where the agents already live), and pesu (Tamil பேசு, “to speak”) is a minimal XS bot — the first thing to run kolu’s own development inside chat.

The short version

kolu is the foundation a chat app integrates — it runs real terminals on machines you control and watches what happens inside them. kolu runs claude, codex, or opencode under any front end, on infrastructure you own. The integration is a mirror of the coordinator: observing comes straight off the daemons (the who-needs-me board), and acting goes through one door — an orchestrator agent in an ordinary kolu terminal. XS — the chat app — keeps everything social: identity, login, presence, attribution. kolu authenticates nothing; the connection is the trust.

The shift: the agent moved into the chat

Karpathy isn’t describing a chatbot you ask questions. He’s describing a coworker: a persistent agent that lives where the team already works, holds the org’s tools and context, and runs tasks on its own while you do something else. You @-tag it, walk away, and it pings you when it needs you. Anthropic shipped this shape as Claude Tag — one shared Claude per channel, tasks it pursues “over hours or days,” an audit log of every task and who asked for it. The proof-point is blunt: “65% of our product team’s code is created by our internal version.” The work moves into chat, and the human’s job shifts from driving keystrokes to managing agents.

In that world the terminal specializes. Chat keeps gaining richer rendering — diffs, highlighting, even little editors — but it stays async text over request and response. It is not a live process you can step into. The terminal is where you drop to a shell, answer an interactive prompt, watch raw output, drive a debugger. Chat owns the breadth; the terminal owns the depth — and kolu is what makes the depth real.

kolu in one picture

At its core kolu does two things: it runs real terminals on computers you control, and watches what’s happening inside them. That core is three parts:

  • kaval owns each live terminal — start an agent, type into it, resize it, kill it. It is also the single point that serializes writes: when input arrives, last one wins.
  • padi is the per-host workspace daemon above it: its agent sensors watch every terminal without touching it, folding the raw noise into a simple board — which agent is working, which is asking you something, which just finished — and it owns the durable session: what each terminal ran, the agent’s resume identity, restore across restarts and even an unclean daemon death.
  • @kolu/surface is the typed wire that carries both over any connection — a local socket, or ssh to another machine. Remote hosts are a shipped, first-class part of the app: add a host and its terminals sit behind a host switcher, on desktop and mobile.

Two things sit either side of kolu, and the relationship with each is different:

  • XS is independent. It already runs without kolu. Integrating kolu is simply what lets a chat thread reach into a real terminal — XS gains the depth, kolu gains a front door. Everything social stays in XS.
  • The machine is wherever kolu runs. kolu runs headlessly on any box — your laptop, a server, or a remote sandboxed host. Remote sandboxes (an Incus cluster, another team’s project) are something it naturally supports: a remote host is just another place to dial the same surface.

So the picture is not a tower of dependencies. XS integrates kolu; kolu runs on whatever machine you choose. The arrow is integration one way and execution the other.

The moat: model-agnostic, open, yours

kolu and a chat app divide cleanly. kolu owns the live process, the files, and the durable session. XS owns identity, login, presence, and who-may-write. A foundation that reaches up and grows chat stops being a neutral base any chat app can integrate and becomes one more single-vendor app. Holding that line isn’t caution — it’s the moat.

The moat — our competitive advantage

kolu runs claude, codex, or opencode under any chat app, on infrastructure you control. That is the bet on open standards and open source, and it is exactly what a single-vendor stack can’t match. Claude Tag is one vendor’s model, with the shell and files hidden inside a cloud sandbox you don’t own. kolu keeps the model swappable, the shell and files real, and the host yours — so the chat app on top is a choice, never a lock-in.

What an agent actually is (Andreessen)

Marc Andreessen, on what decades of agent research quietly converged on: “an agent is … a language model, and above that a bash shell … and then a file system, and the state is stored in files,” plus cron — and “every part of that other than the model is something we already completely know.” The kicker: “your agent is now actually independent of the model … you can swap out a different LLM underneath.”

That is kolu’s architecture, line for line: the shell is the interface to every tool (kolu watches it, doesn’t wrap it), the files are the durable state, and the model is the swappable chip (claude · codex · opencode). A chat app that hard-codes one vendor’s model and hides the shell and files inside a cloud sandbox gives up exactly the durable substance kolu keeps.

The seam: observe out raw, act through the coordinator

XS integrates kolu through one seam with two deliberately asymmetric halves: observe flows out raw; act flows in through one door — the coordinator. kolu authenticates nothing: the connection is the trust — an owner-only socket locally, an ssh link to a remote host — so identity, login, and presence stay in XS.

The coordinator is an orchestrator agent running in an ordinary kolu terminal — the same shape kolu’s own development runs on: one agent that provisions worker terminals, dispatches briefs, answers the workers’ questions, and verifies their claims at the tree. Its behavioral contract is the /orchestrator skill: rulings run through the review lenses with named grounding, teardown kills only recorded PIDs, the human merges every PR. The chat bot is a mirror of that coordinator: it binds one thread to that one terminal, renders the coordinator’s reports into the thread, and relays the thread’s messages back in — attributed per XS identity — using the same drive loop the coordinator itself uses on workers.

Surface Half Reuses
the board out · read-only padi’s agent sensors — which agent is working / asking you / just finished (padi-tui wait’s buckets), rendered straight into the thread with no coordinator hop
attention out · read-only per-terminal urgency through the notify seam — the bot pings the thread instead of the desktop
deep links out a kolu URL to the exact terminal — depth on demand: step in, answer the interactive prompt, debug, in kolu itself
the coordinator bridge in + out one terminal’s screen and input — send a message, wait for the turn to end, read the reply: the identical agent-drives-agent loop kolu already ships

Chat gets no raw act verbs on workers — that absence is the design, not a gap:

  • The write floor dissolves. “At most one writer per terminal” machinery exists only if chat can touch live terminals. With one door, the floor is the coordinator’s inbox: thread messages queue into a conversation and are handled in turn, attributed. Serialization by conversation, not by locks.
  • Guarantees live at the knowing endpoint. The coordinator is the one place that knows campaign state — what is in flight, which merge goes first, what a change must not break — so “who does what next” is decided there, never in a thread reacting to a screen.
  • Discipline is inherited, not re-implemented. Everything the orchestrator contract enforces — claims verified at the tree, grounded rulings, no pattern kills, the human merging — applies to chat traffic automatically, because chat traffic is coordinator traffic.

The same door assists the humans’ own discussion

Because a message to the thread and a message to the coordinator are the same thing, the coordinator is also a participant in the conversation between humans — the teammate shape, not just command-and-control. Several people argue a design in the thread; the coordinator contributes exactly what its contract makes it good at: the claim checked against the actual tree before anyone builds on it, the ruling with its grounding named so the humans can audit the reasoning rather than defer to it, and the running record of what was decided and why. AI-assisted discussion among humans falls out of the coordinator pattern for free — no second bot, no separate “assistant” mode, one attributed inbox.

The first proof: an XS bot

pesu is a small XS bot that binds one XS thread to the coordinator’s terminal: it renders the board and the coordinator’s reports into the thread, and relays the thread’s messages — attributed — as the coordinator’s input. It rides XS’s own identity, presence, and login, and needs no auth in kolu: just the connection.

The milestone is concrete: run kolu’s own development from a thread. kolu is already built this way — a coordinator driving a fleet of worker agents through the exact loop the bot would mirror — so the bot is a renderer of a proven pattern, not new coordination machinery. What pesu proves is the chat half: XS identity mapped to attribution, a thread bound durably to one terminal, and the stream rendered where the team already is.

The target user story, end to end — here replaying a real merged change, PR #1544, which made session export a lightweight chat log: start an agent from a thread, watch it work, get screenshot evidence, jump into the live terminal to try it, then take the PR to green and merge — all without leaving chat. The first milestone lights up the observe half (the stream and the evidence); attaching to test and merging from chat ride the act-in verbs that follow.

The call

kolu is the foundation a chat app integrates — real terminals, durable sessions, an honest read, and one disciplined door for writes: the coordinator. XS owns identity; kolu owns the substance; the coordinator owns the discipline — and lends it to the humans’ own discussion. Build the bridge, prove it with the pesu bot running kolu’s own development in the open, and let any chat app be the front door.
